thread.title: Roaring U.S. jobs market banishes fears of recession, but economy still has soft spots

author: Jeffry Bartash
title: Roaring U.S. jobs market banishes fears of recession, but economy still has soft spots
text:
Bloomberg News/Landov A roaring U.S. jobs engine is powering the economy and provides the strongest bulwark against the threat of recession. A gargantuan 312,000 surge in new jobs in December dispel fears the U.S. faces a looming recession. But it doesn’t mean there’s nothing to worry about.
The increase in jobs in the final month of 2018 was a badly needed salve for a shaken Wall Street after a series of hammered blows wiped out all the stock-market gains for the year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, +3.29% and S&P 500 SPX, +3.43% both posted their biggest annual losses in a decade.
“The report capped the best year of job growth since 2015 and underscores the fact that the economy headed into 2019 with continued strength in the labor market,” said Omair Sharif, senior U.S. economist at Societe Generale.
The cherry on top came when Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell said the central bank would be flexible in when and how much it raised U.S. interest rates . Rising rates also contributed to the market selloff at year end.
The Fed is willing to take a step back because the economy does appear more fragile.
The housing market tailed off toward the second half of 2018, for example, because of higher mortgage rates. And a pair of influential surveys suggested American manufacturers also had a tougher go of it at the end of the year due to a festering trade dispute with China and a slowing global economy.
The standoff with China has already taken a bite out of the hide of U.S. companies and added to a darker tone on Wall Street. Tech giant Apple AAPL, +4.27% last week cut its forecast owing to weaker sales of iPhones, especially in China.
Kevin Hassett, one of President Trump’s economic advisers, said other large U.S. companies that do lots of business in China are also likely to trim sales forecasts.
Lower corporate earnings could muzzle the stock market early 2019, but the worst would only come to pass if companies reduce hiring or even lay off more workers.
Employment gains in December suggest that’s unlikely anytime soon.
Companies are still hiring because of strong demand for their goods and services in the United States. As long as most working-age Americans have a job and the unemployment rate clings near a 49-year low, there’s little chance demand would taper off so sharply that the broader economy is stunted.

The Fed could do its part with a wait-and-see approach to raising interest rates.
Although wages are rising at the fastest pace in a decade, inflation more broadly has eased in the past few months because of falling oil prices and a slower world economy.
“Oil prices have continued to edge lower, contributing to a synchronized easing in inflationary pressures,” economists at Barclays wrote.
An upcoming report on consumer inflation at the end of 2018 is expected to show price pressures may have peaked for now. The consumer price index is forecast to fall slightly in December, potentially slicing the rate of increase over the past 12 months below 2%.
The yearly rate has fallen from a six-year high of 2.9% last summer.
The Fed will also offer a fresh take on how the U.S. economy is performing with its so-called Beige Book due Wednesday.
Jeffry Bartash Jeffry Bartash is a reporter for MarketWatch in Washington.
